claims.text: Without requests, kube-scheduler does not account for a Pod's CPU/memory needs; a container with no memory limit can use memory up to what its node has.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Resource Management for Pods and Containers (requests used by scheduler; if no limit, container could use all memory on the node)

claims.text: kube-scheduler places a Pod only on a node where, for each resource type, the sum of the requests of scheduled containers plus the Pod's requests is within the node's capacity (allocatable).
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Resource Management for Pods and Containers (How Pods with resource requests are scheduled)

claims.text: CPU is measured in cores; 250m (millicores) is 0.25 of a core; memory is in bytes, and Mi is a power-of-two suffix: 256Mi = 256 × 1024 × 1024 bytes.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Resource Management (CPU resource units; Memory resource units)

claims.text: A Pod whose requests fit no node stays Pending with no node assigned, and kube-scheduler records a FailedScheduling event giving the reason (e.g. Insufficient cpu); no image is pulled.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Resource Management (troubleshooting: Pending, FailedScheduling); outputs resources.txt

claims.text: The scheduler uses requests, not actual usage; a container may use less than its request, or more as long as it stays under its limit.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Resource Management ('even if actual memory or CPU resource usage on nodes is very low'; 'can use more than its request')

claims.text: A container over its CPU limit is throttled (slowed), not killed; a container over its memory limit can have a process killed by the kernel OOM killer, reported as OOMKilled, and is then restarted per restartPolicy.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Resource Management (How Kubernetes applies resource requests and limits; OOM)

claims.text: deploy/k8s/api.yaml@stage-2 lines 57-63: api requests cpu 250m, memory 256Mi; limits cpu 500m, memory 512Mi; db, redis, keycloak, mailpit manifests set no resources.
oversized-pod.yaml@stage-2: Pod oversized, caddy:2.10.0, requests cpu "100" (100 cores) and memory 64Mi, more CPU than any node of the kind cluster has.

resources.sh@stage-2 lines 11-27: prints api resources via jsonpath, applies oversized, waits for condition reason Unschedulable, get -o wide, prints the FailedScheduling event message, deletes the Pod.
resources.txt@stage-2: api resources JSON; oversized 0/1 Pending, IP and NODE <none>; event '0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s), 2 Insufficient cpu. ...'.
On the kind cluster the control-plane node is tainted so ordinary Pods are not scheduled there (the 'untolerated taint(s)' part of the event).
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Taints and Tolerations (control-plane NoSchedule taint); kubectl describe node donhang-control-plane

claims.text: kubectl describe node lists each non-terminated Pod with its CPU/memory requests and limits, each followed by a percentage in brackets.
claims.source_hint: kubectl describe node output (Non-terminated Pods; Allocated resources)

claims.text: Requests make the scheduler keep room for each api Pod; with the memory limit a runaway api container is stopped long before it can take all of a node's memory.
Memory limits are enforced by the kernel with OOM kills rather than by slowing the container; the kernel does not throttle memory to keep a container under its limit.
claims.source_hint: kubernetes.io: Resource Management ('memory limits are enforced by the kernel with out of memory (OOM) kills')

claims.text: An event is a record Kubernetes keeps of something that happened to an object (e.g. FailedScheduling for a Pod no node fits).
